# DosKit - Comprehensive Documentation

> A robust, cross-platform foundation for running DOS applications using js-dos WebAssembly technology

## Overview

DosKit is a modern web application that enables users to run classic DOS applications and demos directly in their browser without any installation. Built with cutting-edge web technologies, it provides a seamless, cross-platform DOS emulation experience that works on desktop and mobile devices.

The project leverages js-dos v8.3.20, a WebAssembly-based DOS emulator built on DOSBox. Combined with React 19's modern component architecture and Vite's lightning-fast build system, DosKit delivers an exceptional user experience for retro computing enthusiasts and developers.

DosKit comes with a library of demoscene productions and music trackers, among them Second Reality, Crystal Dream 2, Impulse Tracker and Scream Tracker 3 (see Bundled Applications under Usage). Games are outside its scope.

## Features

### Core Features

- **Interactive DOS Prompt**: The start page boots a fully functional DOS command prompt where users can execute DOS commands, with the application selector open over it
- **Application Library**: Demoscene productions and music trackers, picked from a selector of floppy disks that works with the mouse or the keyboard (arrow keys, Home, End, Space, Enter, Escape; see Basic Usage under Usage)
- **Cross-Platform Compatibility**: Works seamlessly on Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, and Android
- **Progressive Web App (PWA)**: Can be installed as a native app, with offline support
- **Deep Linking**: Load specific applications directly via URL parameters (e.g., `?app=secondreality`)
- **Offline Functionality**: After the first visit the app and its DOS prompt work offline; each application works offline once it has been opened online
- **WebAssembly Performance**: js-dos v8.3.20 runs DOSBox as WebAssembly in a worker thread and renders with WebGL
- **Full Keyboard Support**: All standard DOS keyboard inputs including function keys and special characters
- **Audio Support**: Sound Blaster, Gravis UltraSound and AdLib emulation with proper audio output
- **Responsive Design**: Optimized layouts for desktop, tablet, and mobile devices
- **Fullscreen**: The fullscreen button in the js-dos sidebar makes the player fill the browser window, over DosKit's header and footer; js-dos then narrows its sidebar to a strip on the left, which brings back the button when clicked
- **Touch Controls**: On-screen keyboard in the js-dos sidebar; phones and tablets get DosKit's compact layout first, with js-dos's full keyboard and function-key layout behind its ⎘ key
- **Type-Safe Development**: Full TypeScript support with comprehensive type definitions
- **Service Worker Caching**: js-dos's player and emulator files, and the application archives, stay cached across deploys until js-dos or the archives change, and so do the bundles a deploy leaves unchanged

### PWA Features

- **Installable**: Install DosKit as a native app on desktop and mobile; Firefox on Windows runs it as a web app pinned to the taskbar, from the web apps icon in its address bar. In Chromium browsers, which tell the page when it can be installed, DosKit suggests it 5 seconds after that, waits 7 days after each dismissal, and stops asking after the third
- **Offline Support**: After the first visit the app works offline (see Service Worker under Architecture)
- **Fast Loading**: Service worker caches assets for instant loading
- **Native Experience**: Standalone mode without browser UI
- **Update Prompt**: DosKit checks for a new version every hour and whenever the tab becomes visible again. Once one has installed, it offers to reload into it ("Update Now") or to wait ("Later"); an update put off is offered again on the next visit. The prompt is a modal dialog that gives the keyboard focus to Later, since it can appear while someone types into DOS, and Escape answers Later. Once Update Now in one tab lets the new version take over, every other open tab says that DosKit was updated in another tab and offers Reload or Later, even a tab that had put the update off
- **Connection Status**: An Online/Offline badge in the footer. While the browser reports being offline, whether the connection dropped or the page opened offline, a banner at the top says that the applications opened while online still work and the others need a connection to load; it can be closed, and goes when the connection returns, with a "Back online" notice for 3 seconds

## Technology Stack

### Core Technologies

- **React 19**: Modern UI framework with latest features including concurrent rendering
- **TypeScript 5**: Type-safe JavaScript with strict mode enabled
- **Vite 8**: Next-generation frontend tooling, bundling with Rolldown
- **js-dos 8.3.20**: WebAssembly DOS emulator with DOSBox and DOSBox-X backends; DosKit runs every application on DOSBox
- **retro-floppy**: The floppy disks of the application selector

### Development Tools

- **ESLint**: Code linting with TypeScript support
- **Prettier**: Code formatting, checked in CI
- **Vitest**: Fast unit testing framework, with jsdom and React Testing Library
- **TypeDoc**: API documentation generation
- **Sharp**: High-performance image processing for the PWA icons and social media previews (scripts run by hand)
- **Husky**: Git hooks for pre-commit checks (lint-staged runs ESLint, Prettier and the related tests on staged JavaScript and TypeScript files, and Prettier on the other staged files)

### Why These Technologies?

#### React + Vite
- Fast Development: Hot Module Replacement (HMR) for instant feedback
- Modern Build: Optimized production builds with code splitting
- Developer Experience: Excellent TypeScript integration and tooling
- Rolldown: Vite 8 bundles with Rolldown, a Rust-based bundler that took over from Rollup in Vite; vite.config.ts configures it through build.rolldownOptions

#### js-dos v8.3.20
- Pinned: package.json pins this exact version, and scripts/copy-js-dos.js copies its runtime from node_modules into public/
- WebAssembly: DOSBox compiled to WebAssembly
- Cross-Platform: Works in all modern browsers and Node.js
- Multiple Backends: Supports both DOSBox and DOSBox-X; every DOSBox configuration in DosKit is written for DOSBox
- Active Development: Regular updates and community support

#### TypeScript
- Type Safety: Catch errors at compile time
- Better IDE Support: Autocomplete and inline documentation
- Maintainability: Easier to refactor and scale

## Architecture

### Component Hierarchy

```
StrictMode (main.tsx)
└── ErrorBoundary
    └── App
        ├── OfflineIndicator (offline and back-online notices, install prompt)
        ├── Header (current application, Change Application button)
        ├── ErrorBoundary
        │   └── DosPlayerWithApps
        │       ├── DemoSelector (modal dialog)
        │       │   ├── Notice (an ?app= value that names no app)
        │       │   └── App selection UI
        │       ├── Loading overlay (Cancel)
        │       ├── Error overlay (Try Again, Choose Another Application)
        │       └── DosPlayer (useDosEmulator hook + DosPlayerUI)
        │           └── js-dos emulator instance
        └── Footer (Loading/Ready/Error and Online/Offline badges, Licenses link)
```

UpdateNotification is not part of this tree: src/utils/updatePrompt.ts mounts it in a React root of its own when a new service worker is waiting, or another tab has let one take over.

DosPlayerWithApps reports its status to App, which shows it in the footer's badge: Loading while an application the URL asks for (a deep link, Back and Forward, or Try Again) downloads and while an emulator starts (while the selector downloads an application, the badge keeps the status of the player still running behind it), Ready once js-dos reports the emulator ready, and Error while the load error or the player's start error shows, or once the ErrorBoundary around the player has caught an error. js-dos sends no event when its own download of the emulator's files fails after it has started, so the badge stays at Loading then, while js-dos shows the failure in its own panel. Screen readers announce the badges' changes (a status region).

In development, StrictMode mounts every component twice at once, so each DosPlayer starts js-dos twice in its element: useDosEmulator stops the first start's player and ignores its events, and on a fresh page the adapter holds the second start back until emulators.js, which the first one loads, has run. Production builds mount each component once.

### Data Flow

1. **Application Loading**: User visits site → Service worker serves the page from the network, or from its cache when offline → Loads assets
2. **Emulator Initialization**: DosPlayer component mounts → useDosEmulator starts js-dos with the merged options (DosKit's, then the settings saved from js-dos's settings panel, then the player's own) → js-dos loads the DOSBox backend from /emulators/ → DOSBox initializes with the DOSBox configuration
3. **User Interaction**: User types commands → js-dos processes input → DOSBox executes → Screen updates
4. **Deep Linking**: App id read from `?app=` or the path → URL rewritten to `/?app=<id>` → DosPlayerWithApps downloads the app's ZIP archive and DOSBox configuration → Emulator starts with app, without booting the default prompt first
5. **Selecting an App**: User picks an app in DemoSelector → its archive downloads, with its progress in percent (or in megabytes when the response gives no size), cancellable, and fails if nothing arrives for 20 seconds → DosPlayerWithApps starts a new DosPlayer with the files, also for the app already running, which starts again → the URL becomes `/?app=<id>`, in a new history entry unless it already is (as when the running app is picked again)

### State Management

- React hooks (useState, useEffect, useCallback) for component state, held in App and DosPlayerWithApps and passed down as props; there is no context or global store
- Local storage for the install prompt's dismissals, and for reading the settings js-dos saves from its settings panel (`jsdos.8.*`), through src/utils/storage.ts, which never throws when storage is blocked or full
- URL parameters for deep linking state

### Service Worker

`public/sw.js` is registered in production builds only:

- **Install**: precaches the app shell (/, which serves index.html, the manifest, logo and favicon), every JS and CSS bundle, including the lazily loaded app configs, and js-dos: its player (js-dos.js, js-dos.css) and the DOSBox backend (wdosbox, wlibzip and emulators.js). A bundle that an earlier deploy's cache holds under the same name is copied from there instead of downloaded, and only the js-dos files missing from the cache of their version are downloaded
- **Pages**: network first with a 5-second timeout; when the network fails or times out, every URL gets the index.html install stored, so deep links open offline too. Pages fetched online are not stored
- **Bundles** (`/assets/`): cache first; a bundle's name changes with its content, so a cached copy never goes stale
- **js-dos's files** (`/js-dos.js`, `/js-dos.css` and `/emulators/`): cache first, from a cache named after the js-dos version, which deploys keep, and never refreshed, so a page gets the player and the emulator files of the js-dos its worker installed until a worker with another js-dos version takes over, after which its next player can get that version's emulator files until it reloads; DOSBox-X is not precached and is stored on first use
- **Application archives** (`/demos/*.zip`): cache first, from a cache named after a hash of the archives, which deploys keep while the archives stay the same; each is stored on first use
- **Other assets** (the manifest, the logo and icons): stale-while-revalidate, in a cache of at most 100 entries that trims the least recently used, never the precached files
- **Updates**: a build that changes a file the site serves, or the worker, installs as a new worker, which waits until the user accepts the update prompt or every tab of the app has closed. The worker's cache version is a hash of the built site, so a build that changes neither, such as one after a change to the README alone, writes the same worker and offers no update

### Error Handling

- **Error boundaries** around the whole app (main.tsx) and around the player (App.tsx), which report to the error tracker; the one around the player also sets the footer's badge to Error
- **Global handler** (src/utils/globalErrorHandler.ts): reports uncaught errors and unhandled promise rejections to the error tracker, whose report is the one line logged for each (the browser still reports the error itself), and keeps known harmless ones out of the console: js-dos's keyboard lock calls that fail without a user gesture, keyboard lock requests that a newer one superseded (two players starting milliseconds apart), ResizeObserver loop notices and browser extension errors
- **Error tracking** (src/utils/errorTracking.ts): a console tracker; no remote service is set up
- **Downloads**: the request for an application archive retries network failures and 408, 429, 500, 502, 503 and 504 responses up to three times with exponential backoff, but a network failure while the browser reports being offline fails at once, and so does one while the archive itself arrives. A download fails as a timeout when no data arrives for 20 seconds, counted from the request, from each retry, from the response and from each chunk of the archive, so one that keeps receiving data has no time limit; and a response that is not a ZIP archive is refused (Vite's dev and preview servers answer a missing archive with index.html). A download the user cancels, or a newer navigation supersedes, is not reported as an error
- **Messages**: the selector and the error box of an application the URL asks for (a deep link, or Back and Forward) explain a failed load with the same messages (cannot connect, not available offline yet, file not found, too many requests, server unavailable, took too long, unable to load the application archive), with the technical message under a collapsed Details line; an `?app=` value that names no app opens the selector with a notice above the disks that the application was not found; the loading overlay's Cancel stops the download and does what Choose Another Application does; the error box's Try Again, which has the keyboard focus, downloads the application again, and its Choose Another Application opens the selector over the DOS prompt; and the player shows why, with a Reload Page button, when js-dos cannot start, such as when js-dos.js did not load, or emulators.js, which js-dos loads when the first player starts, failed to download or did not set up the emulator. The next player to start, such as one for an application picked in the selector, downloads emulators.js again

## Installation & Setup

### Prerequisites

- Node.js 24 or later (package.json engines; the version is in .nvmrc)
- npm (the repository's lockfile is package-lock.json)
- Modern browser with WebAssembly support

### Installation Steps

1. Clone the repository:
```bash
git clone https://github.com/cameronrye/doskit.git
cd doskit
```

2. Install dependencies:
```bash
npm install
```

3. Start the development server (it first copies the js-dos runtime from node_modules into public/):
```bash
npm run dev
```

4. Open your browser and navigate to `http://localhost:5173`

The DOS emulator will automatically load and present an interactive DOS prompt, with the application selector open over it!

The service worker is only registered in production builds: to try offline behavior, run `npm run build` and `npm run preview`.

## Configuration

### DOSBox Configuration

DosKit uses DOSBox configuration files to customize the DOS environment. The default configuration, which the DOS prompt boots with, is located in `src/config/dosbox.conf.ts`; each application builds its own in its config module in `src/dos-apps/`, starting from a preset in `src/utils/dosboxConfigBuilder.ts`.

js-dos's default DOSBox backend ignores settings it does not have without a warning, such as `core=dynamic`, a 486 or Pentium `cputype`, `[dos] ver` or a `[memory]` section; `src/dos-apps/README.md` lists them.

Example custom configuration:
```typescript
const customConfig = `
[cpu]
core=auto
cycles=max

[autoexec]
@echo off
echo Welcome to My DOS App!
mount c .
c:
myapp.exe
`;
```

### js-dos Options

Customize the emulator behavior with js-dos options in `src/config/jsdos.config.ts`. DosKit's defaults: the DOSBox backend in a worker thread, WebGL rendering at a 4:3 aspect ratio, soft fullscreen, volume 0.7, autoStart with no countdown, js-dos cloud features off (`noCloud`), and emulator files from `/emulators/`.

The volume, mouse sensitivity, aspect ratio, image rendering, theme and on-screen controls' scale chosen in js-dos's settings panel win over DosKit's: js-dos saves them in localStorage (`jsdos.8.*`), and DosKit passes the saved values at every start, so they last through app switches and reloads. js-dos saves DosKit's own values the same way at the first start, so a change to those defaults reaches only browsers that have not run DosKit before. The panel's Mirror controls has no option to pass, so a new player goes back to the value js-dos read when the page loaded.

Available options:
- `theme`: A js-dos theme, such as 'dark' (DosKit's default) or 'light'
- `volume`: 0.0 to 1.0
- `fullScreen`: Start in the browser's fullscreen. js-dos applies it before `softFullscreen`, through the browser's Fullscreen API, which browsers only allow just after a click or key press. DosKit leaves it unset, so js-dos makes no Fullscreen API call: even `false` has it call `document.exitFullscreen()` at every start, which rejects outside fullscreen
- `softFullscreen`: Have the fullscreen button in the js-dos sidebar make the player fill the browser window, instead of asking the browser's Fullscreen API; DosKit sets it
- `autoStart`: Auto-start emulator on load
- `backend`: 'dosbox' or 'dosboxX' (DosKit's DOSBox configurations are written for 'dosbox')
- `mouseCapture`: Auto-capture mouse input
- `initFs`: The files to start with: a ZIP archive as a `Uint8Array`, one `{ path, contents }` file, or a list of archives and files. js-dos writes the files first, then unpacks the archives in list order, so an archive's files replace those of the archives before it and any listed file at the same path
- See `src/types/js-dos.d.ts` for the options DosKit declares; it leaves out js-dos's IPX networking options (`ipx`, `ipxBackend`, `room` and `noNetworking`)

### Mobile Configuration

DosKit detects mobile devices by their user agent and applies `mobileJsDosConfig` from `src/config/jsdos.config.ts`, which gives the on-screen keyboard (the keyboard button in the js-dos sidebar) three layouts. The ⎘ key on each switches to the next, and from the last back to the first:
1. DosKit's compact layout, shown first: Esc, F1, F2, F3 and F5; 1 to 5 and Backspace; the left-hand letters q w e r t, a s d f g and z x c v b; ⎘, Ctrl, Alt, Space and Enter; and the arrow keys
2. js-dos's full keyboard: every letter and digit, Esc, Tab, Shift, Ctrl, Alt, Space, Backspace, Enter, the arrow keys and ` - = ( ) { } [ ] \ ; : ' , . /
3. js-dos's function-key layout: F1 to F12, Esc, 0 to 9, { } ( ), Shift, Ctrl, Alt, Space, PgUp, PgDown, Backspace, Del, Tab, the arrow keys, a keypad whose digits but 5 and 0 are labeled as arrows, and - + . Enter

All three label their keys as js-dos does (␛ Esc, ⌫ Backspace, ↵ Enter, ⇑ Shift). js-dos presses nothing for the \ and / keys of its own full keyboard, and keypad 0 for its ` key, so DosKit's copy names those keys Ü, ¿ and À, which js-dos presses as \ / and `, and labels them \ / and `. It leaves out js-dos's En/Ru key, which switches the labels to Russian. Safari on iPadOS identifies itself as a Mac by default, so an iPad in Safari gets the desktop settings and js-dos's own two layouts, the function-key layout first.

## Usage

### Basic Usage

Visit https://doskit.net/ to use the emulator directly in your browser. DosKit boots to an interactive DOS prompt where you can execute DOS commands, and opens the application selector over it: pick an application to run it, or close the selector to use the prompt.

In the selector, click a disk to see its details and Load Application, or double-click it to load it at once. With the keyboard, Tab reaches the disks as a single stop; the arrow keys, Home and End move between them and select them (during a download they only move the focus), Space selects the focused disk, Enter loads it, and Escape cancels a download, or else closes the selector. Choosing another disk while one downloads, with Space or a click, cancels that download, and loading another, with Enter or a double-click, replaces it. Tab and Shift+Tab stay inside the selector. Picking the application that is running starts it again.

Keys pressed on DosKit's own controls (the selector, the header's button, the notices, the update prompt and the footer's links) stay with those controls and never reach the running program. Once the focus is on the page, such as after a pick or a click on the DOS screen, every key goes to DOS, Tab included: to use DosKit's controls again, click one. A key's release goes where its press went, whatever has the focus when the key comes up.

### Bundled Applications

`src/config/apps.config.ts` registers these, and each opens at its link:

- Second Reality (Future Crew, 1993): https://doskit.net/?app=secondreality
- Impulse Tracker (Jeffrey Lim, 1997): https://doskit.net/?app=impulsetracker
- Starport BBS Intro II (Future Crew, 1993): https://doskit.net/?app=starportbbstro
- Scream Tracker 3 (Future Crew, 1994): https://doskit.net/?app=screamtracker
- Unreal (Future Crew, 1992): https://doskit.net/?app=unreal
- Panic (Future Crew, 1993): https://doskit.net/?app=panic
- Squid BBS Intro (cld & The Doctor, 1994): https://doskit.net/?app=squidbbstro
- 3D Rotation Demo (Draeden of VLA, 1993): https://doskit.net/?app=3drotate
- Starfield Effect (Draeden of VLA, 1993): https://doskit.net/?app=stars
- Crystal Dream 2 (Triton, 1993): https://doskit.net/?app=crystaldream2

While Impulse Tracker or Scream Tracker 3 runs, closing or reloading the page asks first. A song in progress lives only in the emulator's memory, as does any file saved inside an application, and is gone once another player starts or the page reloads; and on Windows, Linux and ChromeOS browsers keep Ctrl+W, Ctrl+N and Ctrl+T for themselves, so there Scream Tracker 3's Ctrl-W (save) would close the tab (macOS browsers use ⌘ for these, and Ctrl+W reaches DOS).

### Deep Linking

DosKit supports loading specific applications directly via URL parameters:

- Load Second Reality: `https://doskit.net/?app=secondreality`
- Load Impulse Tracker: `https://doskit.net/?app=impulsetracker`

Features:
- Shareable Links: URLs automatically update when you select an app
- Bookmarkable: Save direct links to your favorite DOS applications
- Browser Navigation: Back and Forward load the application in the URL; the running one stops, sound and all, as soon as the next one starts downloading, and going back to the start URL returns to the DOS prompt with the selector open
- Refresh-Safe: Page refreshes maintain the loaded application
- Error Handling: an `?app=` value that names no app, an empty one included, opens the selector with a notice above the disks that the application was not found, and is removed from the address bar; the notice goes once the selector closes or an application loads. A path that names no app opens the start page
- One URL Form: path-style links (`https://doskit.net/secondreality`) and other spellings (`?app=second-reality`) open the same app, and the address bar is rewritten to `/?app=secondreality`
- Direct Start: a deep link downloads its application and starts it without booting the default prompt first; the Cancel button under "Loading application..." stops the download and opens the selector over the DOS prompt instead

### Adding DOS Applications

An application in the selector is three pieces, and `src/dos-apps/README.md` walks through each:

1. A ZIP archive of the program's files at `public/demos/<id>.zip`
2. A config module, `src/dos-apps/<id>.config.ts`, with the archive's URL and the DOSBox configuration, built from a preset in `src/utils/dosboxConfigBuilder.ts`
3. An entry in `availableApps` in `src/config/apps.config.ts`, which imports the config module lazily

The guide also has the application recorded in more places: a row in the table of `public/demos/README.md`, and an entry there with what the ZIP holds, its size in bytes and MD5, and the archive's source, year, authors and terms; a line in this file's Bundled Applications list; ROADMAP.md's list of the applications and its three counts of them; and `docs/SCENERS.md`, for a program from the sceners organization.

`npx vitest run src/config/apps.config.test.ts` checks every registered application: that its archive is a ZIP in `public/demos`, that its DOSBox configuration leaves out the settings the default backend ignores, and that its description and banner give no other release year than its registry entry. It also checks that every archive in `public/demos` belongs to an application and that `public/demos/README.md` records the archive's size and MD5 as they are. Only add programs you may redistribute.

### Programmatic Control

Access the Command Interface for programmatic control:

```typescript
import { useState } from 'react';
import { DosPlayer } from './components/DosPlayer';
import type { CommandInterface } from './types/js-dos';

function MyApp() {
  const [ci, setCi] = useState<CommandInterface | null>(null);

  const handleReady = (commandInterface: CommandInterface) => {
    setCi(commandInterface);

    // Now you can control DOS programmatically
    commandInterface.simulateKeyPress(257); // Press Enter (257 in js-dos key codes)
  };

  return (
    <>
      <DosPlayer onReady={handleReady} onExit={() => setCi(null)} />
      <button onClick={() => ci?.pause()} disabled={!ci}>
        Pause
      </button>
    </>
  );
}
```

`onExit` is called once for each `onReady`: when DOS exits, or when the player is unmounted.

Available commands:
- `ci.pause()` / `ci.resume()` - Control emulation
- `ci.mute()` / `ci.unmute()` - Audio control
- `ci.screenshot()` - Capture screen
- `ci.fsReadFile()` / `ci.fsWriteFile()` - File system access

## API Documentation

### DosPlayer Component

Main component for DOS emulation. It starts js-dos once per mount and stops it on unmount, so give it a new `key` to run something else.

Props:
- `dosboxConf?: string` - DOSBox configuration (default: the DOS prompt's, from `src/config/dosbox.conf.ts`)
- `options?: Partial<DosOptions>` - js-dos options, merged over the defaults in `src/config/jsdos.config.ts`
- `onReady?: (ci: CommandInterface) => void` - Callback when emulator is ready
- `onExit?: () => void` - Callback when a ready emulator is gone, because DOS exited or unmounting stopped it; called once per onReady
- `onError?: (error: string) => void` - Callback when the emulator cannot start, with the error the player shows
- `className?: string` - CSS class name
- `style?: React.CSSProperties` - Inline styles

### CommandInterface

Interface for controlling the DOS emulator programmatically (the full interface, as js-dos's emulators package declares it, is in `src/types/js-dos.d.ts`).

Methods:
- `pause(): void` - Pause emulation
- `resume(): void` - Resume emulation
- `mute(): void` - Mute audio
- `unmute(): void` - Unmute audio
- `screenshot(): Promise<ImageData>` - Capture screenshot
- `fsReadFile(file: string): Promise<Uint8Array>` - Read file from DOS filesystem
- `fsWriteFile(file: string, contents: ReadableStream<Uint8Array> | Uint8Array): Promise<void>` - Write file to DOS filesystem
- `persist(onlyChanges?: boolean): Promise<Uint8Array | PersistedSockdrives | null>` - Pack the DOS filesystem's changes (or, with `false`, all of it) into a bundle, or null when nothing is packed. With `onlyChanges`, the default, a bundle that mounts sockdrives resolves to `{ drives: { url, persist }[] }` instead, the changes of each drive
- `simulateKeyPress(...keyCodes: number[]): void` - Simulate key presses, in js-dos key codes rather than the browser's: Enter is 257 and Esc 256, while letters (uppercase) and digits keep their ASCII codes
- `exit(): Promise<void>` - Exit emulator

## Development

### Available Scripts

```bash
# List all scripts by category, with the command each one runs
npm run help

# Start development server (copies js-dos into public/ first)
npm run dev

# Build for production (copies js-dos, type-checks, bundles, stamps the service worker)
npm run build

# Preview production build (http://localhost:4173)
npm run preview

# Run linter
npm run lint

# Format files, or only check their formatting (as CI does)
npm run format
npm run format:check

# Run tests once
npm run test

# Run tests in watch mode
npm run test:watch

# Run tests with UI
npm run test:ui

# Run tests with coverage
npm run test:coverage

# Regenerate the PWA icons (not part of the build)
npm run generate-icons

# Regenerate social media images after editing their SVGs (not part of the build)
npm run generate-social-images

# Generate API documentation (into docs/api)
npm run docs

# Watch API documentation
npm run docs:watch
```

### Development Workflow

1. Start the dev server: `npm run dev`
2. Make changes: Edit files in `src/`
3. See changes instantly: Vite HMR updates the browser automatically
4. Test: Interact with the DOS prompt to verify functionality
5. Build: Run `npm run build` to create production bundle

### Testing

DosKit uses Vitest for unit testing, with jsdom and React Testing Library. Tests sit next to the code they cover, `src/integration/` holds integration tests that render the whole app with js-dos faked, and `scripts/*.test.js` test the build scripts, run the service worker in a sandbox, and check 404.html, robots.txt, the licenses page, the icons, index.html's metadata and the ESLint configuration. `tsc -b` type-checks the tests too (tsconfig.test.json).

```bash
# Run tests once
npm run test

# Run tests in watch mode
npm run test:watch

# Run tests with UI
npm run test:ui

# Generate coverage report
npm run test:coverage
```

### Code Style

The project follows strict TypeScript and ESLint rules:

- Strict TypeScript mode enabled
- ESLint with React hooks plugin; it also lints the scripts in scripts/ and the service worker, public/sw.js
- Prettier for code formatting
- Husky for pre-commit hooks

See docs/STYLE_GUIDE.md for detailed coding standards.

## Deployment

DosKit is configured for automatic deployment to GitHub Pages with custom domain support.

### Quick Deployment

1. Enable GitHub Pages in repository settings (Settings → Pages → Source: GitHub Actions)
2. Push to main branch: `git push origin main`
3. Monitor deployment: Check the Actions tab
4. Visit your site: `https://doskit.net/`

The site automatically rebuilds and deploys on every push to `main`, once the CI jobs pass: lint, format check, type check, tests, the build with a check of its CSS against the oldest supported browsers (scripts/check-built-css.js), and an audit that fails on a high or critical advisory in a production dependency (`npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high`; the audit of all dependencies only reports).

### Releases

release-please keeps a release pull request open from the conventional commits on `main`. Merging it bumps the version in package.json, adds the release to CHANGELOG.md and publishes a GitHub release, to which the release workflow attaches a ZIP of the build.

### Custom Domain Setup

1. Enter your domain under Settings → Pages → Custom domain. With GitHub Actions as the source, GitHub ignores any CNAME file, so `public/CNAME` does not set the domain
2. Configure DNS records to point to GitHub Pages
3. Enable HTTPS in GitHub Pages settings (Enforce HTTPS, once GitHub offers it)

### Build Process

The build process (`npm run build`) includes:
1. Copying the js-dos runtime from node_modules into public/ (scripts/copy-js-dos.js, run as prebuild)
2. TypeScript type checking of the app, the config files and the tests (`tsc -b`)
3. Vite production build with code splitting (each application's config module is a chunk of its own, and so is React), asset optimization and minification, for the oldest supported browsers (build.target in vite.config.ts); the licenses of the packages it bundles go to licenses/third-party-licenses.txt
4. 404.html, written as a copy of index.html, so that GitHub Pages boots the app for path-style deep links such as /secondreality
5. Service worker version injection (scripts/inject-sw-version.js): a cache version that is a hash of the built site and the worker, so it changes only when they do; the js-dos version and a hash of the application archives, which name the caches deploys keep; and the list of bundles to precache. The build fails if the worker would precache a file that is not in dist/.

The social media images are not part of the build: after editing their SVG sources, run `npm run generate-social-images` and commit the PNGs.

## Browser Compatibility

### Desktop Browsers

- Chrome/Edge 98+ (Recommended)
- Firefox 94+
- Safari 15.4+
- Opera 84+

### Mobile Browsers

- Safari on iOS and iPadOS 15.4+
- Chrome and Firefox on Android, from the same versions as on the desktop

These are the first versions with `structuredClone()`, which js-dos's player calls once a second while it runs; in older browsers each call ends in an error. The build writes DosKit's JavaScript and CSS for these versions (build.target in vite.config.ts), and CI checks the built CSS against them.

### Requirements

- WebAssembly support (required)
- JavaScript enabled
- Minimum 2GB RAM recommended
- Modern GPU for WebGL rendering (optional but recommended)

### Feature Support Matrix

| Feature | Chrome 98+ | Firefox 94+ | Safari 15.4+ | Edge 98+ | Mobile |
|---------|------------|-------------|--------------|----------|--------|
| WebAssembly | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Service Workers | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| PWA Install | Yes | 143+ on Windows | 17+ | Yes | Yes |
| Audio | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Touch Controls | N/A | N/A | N/A | N/A | Partial |
| Offline Mode | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |

Touch Controls are partial on mobile because js-dos draws the on-screen keyboard inside the player, under the DOS screen, without scrolling, so on a short player the bottom rows of a layout are cut off: on an upright phone the size of an iPhone 13, the function-key layout's keypad, all four of its rows while an app runs (at the DOS prompt, whose header is shorter, the last three, one of them partly), and held sideways, the compact layout's bottom row, its ← ↓ → keys. The fullscreen button in the js-dos sidebar gives the player the whole window, where every layout fits on such a phone. js-dos's own layouts, which desktop browsers and iPads in Safari get, press nothing for their \ and / keys and keypad 0 for `.

DosKit's fullscreen is js-dos's soft fullscreen, which makes the player fill the window with CSS and calls no Fullscreen API. js-dos also asks for a keyboard lock (of W and Escape) at every start, but the browsers that have the Keyboard Lock API, Chromium ones such as Chrome and Edge, apply a lock only in the fullscreen the Fullscreen API starts, so it never takes effect in DosKit: browsers keep their shortcuts for themselves, such as Ctrl+W, Ctrl+N and Ctrl+T on Windows and Linux (⌘W, ⌘N and ⌘T on macOS).

## Troubleshooting

### Common Issues

#### "DOS emulator library not loaded"
- js-dos.js comes from DosKit's own site (/js-dos.js), not a CDN: check the browser console and network panel for that request
- Check internet connection
- Try refreshing the page
- Clear browser cache
- In a local checkout, `npm run dev` and `npm run build` copy js-dos into public/ first; if that step reports that js-dos is not installed, run `npm ci`

#### "The DOS emulator could not be loaded"
- /emulators/emulators.js, which js-dos loads when the first player starts, failed to download, or ran without setting the emulator up
- Check internet connection, then click Reload Page in the player (after the first visit, the service worker serves the file offline)
- Or pick an application in the selector: the next player to start downloads emulators.js again
- Check the browser console and network panel for /emulators/emulators.js

#### Black Screen / Emulator Not Starting
- Check browser console for errors
- Verify WebAssembly support
- Try a different browser
- Disable browser extensions
- Check hardware acceleration

#### Poor Performance / Lag
- Reduce CPU cycles in DOSBox config
- Enable hardware acceleration
- Close other browser tabs
- Try different rendering backend
- Reduce screen resolution

#### Keyboard Not Working
- Click the DOS screen: keys pressed while one of DosKit's controls has the focus, such as the selector, the header's button or a footer link (also after it has opened a tab), go to that control, not to DOS
- Check browser has focus
- Use on-screen keyboard on mobile
- Check console for errors

#### Audio Not Playing
- Audio automatically unmutes when ready
- Check browser audio not muted
- Verify volume setting in options
- Click inside emulator for user interaction
- Check DOSBox sound card configuration

#### Application Fails to Load
- Check internet connection: while the browser reports being online, downloads retry network failures up to three times, though not one while the archive itself arrives, and a download fails when no data arrives for 20 seconds ("The request took too long to complete"); while it reports being offline, they fail at once
- Offline, only applications that have been opened online before can load; any other shows "This application isn't available offline yet", and opening it once online stores it
- After a failed deep link or Back and Forward, Try Again downloads the application again (offline, for one not stored yet, it fails again at once), and Choose Another Application opens the selector over the DOS prompt

### Debug Mode

Enable detailed logging in development:
```typescript
import { logger } from './utils/logger';
logger.debug('MyComponent', 'Debug message');
```

The logger prints every level, with timestamps, in development; production builds keep warnings and errors.
